SK2032 Remove GC.SuppressFinalize from a type with no finalizer

GC.SuppressFinalize(this) is called from a sealed class that declares no finalizer and derives directly from object, so there is no finalizer anywhere to suppress.

CategoryCorrectness
Default severitysuggestion
ScopeSemantic
Needs a compilationyes
Runs under --load=looseno
Cached per fileyes
Fixyes, safe
Language version floor—
Since1.3
ReSharperGCSuppressFinalizeForTypeWithoutDestructor (resharper_gc_suppress_finalize_for_type_without_destructor_highlighting)

Why

The call is copied out of the canonical Dispose pattern into types that never had a finalizer. It costs nothing at runtime and reads as though the type has one, which sends the next reader looking for a finalizer that is not there. Deleting the statement is the whole repair.

Example

Instead of:

sealed class Reader : IDisposable {
    public void Dispose() {
        stream.Dispose();
        GC.SuppressFinalize(this);
    }
}

Write:

sealed class Reader : IDisposable {
    public void Dispose() => stream.Dispose();
}

The ReSharper mapping

The export sets resharper_gc_suppress_finalize_for_type_without_destructor_highlighting to warning and Skala defaults the rule to suggestion, so --resharper-severities raises it. The lower default is deliberate: the call is harmless at runtime, so this is source noise rather than a defect, and a gate that fails on it would fail on tidiness.

When it does not fire

Reported only for GC.SuppressFinalize(this) written as a statement directly inside a block, in a sealed class that derives straight from object and declares no finalizer in a single non-partial declaration. Every part of that is load-bearing. ⚠ An unsealed type is excluded because a derived type may declare a finalizer, which makes the base's call the thing that suppresses it; a type with any base class other than object is excluded for the same reason one level up. A partial or multi-file declaration is excluded so the answer stays decidable from the file the finding is in, which is what scope: Semantic promises the cache. Structs are excluded: they cannot have finalizers at all, so the call is redundant there too, but it also boxes and that is a different finding. An argument that is not literally this, a call in an expression-bodied member, and a call as an embedded statement under an if are all excluded, because the fix is a deletion and each of those has no statement to delete or leaves a construct behind that does not compile. Reflection or a runtime-registered finalizer is outside the proof.
